title: Representing Electronic Systems
description: System block diagrams, open and closed loop systems, circuit schematics, and PCB layouts explained.
content_html:
Why We Use Different Representations

Electronic systems can be represented in three different ways: system block diagrams, circuit schematics, and PCB layouts. Each method has a different purpose and level of detail. A block diagram gives an overview of what a system does; a schematic shows exactly which components are used and how they connect; a PCB layout shows where components are physically placed on a board. The OCR specification requires you to interpret — and partially complete — all three types, for systems with up to four blocks.

System Block Diagrams and the Systems Approach

The systems approach breaks any electronic system into three fundamental stages: input, process, and output. In a block diagram, each stage is drawn as a labelled rectangle, and arrows show the direction of signal flow between blocks. A simple torch system might show: battery (input) → switch (process) → LED (output). Block diagrams are quick to draw and easy to understand, making them ideal for planning and communicating a design before any components are chosen.

A key distinction the specification requires is between open loop systems and closed loop systems. In an open loop system, information flows only in one direction from input to output; there is no feedback. A microwave oven set to run for two minutes regardless of food temperature is open loop — the output (heated food) does not influence the input. In a closed loop system, a feedback loop carries information from the output back to the input. A central heating thermostat is closed loop: the room temperature (output) is fed back and compared with the set temperature (input) to switch the boiler on or off.

Key Fact

Open loop: input → process → output (no feedback). Closed loop: input → process → output, plus a feedback arrow from output back to input. Signal arrows in block diagrams must always show the direction of signal flow. The OCR specification tests you on interpreting and completing block diagrams with up to four blocks.

Circuit Schematics

A circuit schematic (also called a circuit diagram) uses standardised symbols to represent components and shows how they are electrically connected. Every component has a specific symbol — a resistor is shown as a rectangle (BS standard) or a zigzag (US standard); an LED as a diode symbol with two outward arrows; a battery as long and short alternating lines. Schematics do not show the physical size or location of components — they focus purely on the electrical connections. When interpreting a schematic, trace each connection to identify the circuit topology (series or parallel) and the function of each component.

PCB Layouts

A printed circuit board (PCB) layout shows the actual physical arrangement of components and the copper tracks that connect them on the board. Unlike a schematic, a PCB layout is drawn to scale and shows where each component is soldered. PCB design software produces both the schematic and the corresponding PCB layout; the layout is then used to manufacture the physical board. When reading a PCB layout, components are identified by reference designators (R1 for first resistor, C1 for first capacitor, etc.), and copper tracks appear as solid lines or polygons connecting pads.

Key Fact

Block diagram: shows system function and signal flow, no component detail. Circuit schematic: shows component types and electrical connections using standard symbols. PCB layout: shows physical size, position, and copper track routing of every component on the board. Each representation serves a different stage of the engineering design process.

When an OCR exam question asks you to complete a block diagram, follow these steps: (1) Identify which blocks are already drawn and what stage they represent (input, process, output, or feedback). (2) Identify what is missing — a block label, a signal arrow, or a feedback path. (3) For each empty box, ask: is it converting an environmental signal into an electrical signal? If so, it is an input/sensor. Is it controlling or switching another component? That is a process block. Is it converting electrical energy into light, sound or movement? That is an output. (4) Draw signal arrows between every block to show the direction of signal flow — arrows on the feedback path must point from output back towards input. Always use a ruler and label every block clearly.

A freezer temperature alarm is a classic closed loop example for the exam. Input: NTC thermistor senses temperature. Process: microcontroller compares measured temperature with a threshold. Output: buzzer sounds if temperature is too high. Feedback: the microcontroller continuously reads the thermistor output, so the system self-regulates — it checks and re-checks the temperature rather than acting once and stopping. This feedback loop makes the system closed loop. In the block diagram, draw the feedback arrow from the output stage back to the process block, with an arrow pointing towards the process block.
exam_tip_html: Questions on block diagrams often ask you to state whether a system is open or closed loop and justify your answer — you must refer to the presence or absence of a feedback path, not just say 'there is/isn't feedback'. For schematic questions, use the standard BS circuit symbol names (e.g. 'NPN transistor', 'LED', 'thermistor') — vague descriptions like 'a triangle shape' will not gain marks. When completing PCB or schematic questions, check that every component connects to both the positive and the negative supply line, or the circuit will not be complete.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Three representation methods serve different purposes: block diagrams show system function and signal flow; schematics show component connections using standard symbols; PCB layouts show physical size and copper track routing.
  • Open loop systems have no feedback path — input, process, output only. Closed loop systems include a feedback arrow from output back to input, allowing the system to self-regulate.
  • To complete a partially drawn block diagram, identify each block's stage (input, process, output, or feedback), add missing labels and signal arrows in the correct direction, and check the arrow on any feedback path points back towards the process block.

glossary_terms.definition: A simplified diagram that shows a system as a series of labelled rectangles connected by arrows, without showing individual components.
A system in which there is no feedback path — the output has no influence on the input or the processing stage.
A system in which part of the output is fed back to the input to adjust and regulate the system's behaviour.
A standardised diagram that uses agreed circuit symbols to show how components are connected in an electronic circuit.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a characteristic of a closed loop system?
A) The output has no effect on the input.
B) There are no process blocks.
C) A feedback path returns information from output to input.
D) The system operates only once.
practice_questions.marks: C) A feedback path returns information from output to input. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between a circuit schematic and a PCB layout.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: a schematic uses standard symbols / a PCB layout shows physical component positions; a schematic does not show size or scale / a PCB layout is drawn to scale; a schematic shows electrical connections only / a PCB layout shows copper tracks and pad positions; reference designators (R1, C1) identify components on a PCB layout. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an open loop and a closed loop system. Use an example of each in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: open loop — no feedback; output does not affect the input (e.g. a microwave set to a fixed time). 1 mark: closed loop — output is fed back to the input/process stage to regulate behaviour (e.g. a thermostat comparing room temperature to set temperature). 1 mark: clear comparison or development — in the closed loop example, the feedback means the system continuously adjusts, whereas in the open loop example the system acts once without checking the result. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of a system block diagram and explain what the signal arrows on the diagram represent. Give one advantage of using a block diagram over a circuit schematic.
practice_questions.marks:
Purpose (1 mark): a block diagram shows the overall function and stages of a system (input → process → output) without detail of individual components.
Signal arrows (1 mark): signal arrows show the direction in which information or signals flow between blocks (including the direction of any feedback path).
Advantage (2 marks): a block diagram is quicker to draw and easier to understand than a schematic, making it ideal for the early planning stage of a design when component choices have not yet been made — it communicates what the system does, not how it is built (2 marks for a developed advantage with reason; 1 mark for a brief advantage only). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is designing an automatic garden watering system. The system should monitor soil moisture and turn on a pump when moisture falls below a set level. When moisture returns to the correct level the pump switches off.

Discuss which type of system — open loop or closed loop — is more suitable for this application, and how it should be represented as a block diagram.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): clear identification that closed loop is required (1 mark); explanation that the moisture sensor output must be fed back to the process stage so the pump is switched off when moisture is restored — without feedback the pump would simply run for a fixed time regardless of actual soil moisture, potentially over- or under-watering (developed argument for closed loop, 2 marks); block diagram description: moisture sensor (input) → microcontroller/comparator (process) → water pump (output), with a feedback arrow from the output/moisture reading back to the process block and signal arrows showing direction of flow (block diagram description, 2 marks); acknowledgement that an open loop system would be simpler and cheaper but would not respond to actual conditions (consideration of the counter-argument, 1 mark).
Secure (3–4 marks): identifies closed loop correctly, explains feedback, attempts block diagram description.
Developing (2 marks): identifies correct system type but limited justification or block diagram description.
Emerging (1 mark): a single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
An engineering company is producing a new smart home security system. The design team must choose between representing the system using block diagrams, circuit schematics, or PCB layouts at different stages of the design process.

Evaluate the importance of using all three representation methods across the full design and production process of the security system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): a balanced evaluation recognising that each method is most valuable at a different stage. Block diagram: essential at the concept stage — the team can agree on system function (sensor inputs, microcontroller process, siren/light output, feedback for arming) without committing to components; stakeholders (non-technical) can read it easily (developed, with example from security system). Circuit schematic: essential at the detailed design stage — specifies exact components (PIR sensor, NPN transistor driver, relay, 12 V siren), allows electrical checking (correct connections, appropriate component ratings), and forms the reference document for building and testing prototypes (developed). PCB layout: essential at the production stage — determines physical board size, track routing, and component placement for manufacture; an error in the PCB layout will produce a non-functional board even if the schematic is correct (developed). Evaluation: no single representation is sufficient on its own; using all three in sequence reduces errors by progressively adding detail, and omitting any stage risks expensive mistakes. A clear judgement: all three methods are equally important but serve different engineering audiences and stages — block diagrams communicate function, schematics communicate design, and PCB layouts communicate manufacture.
Secure (5–6 marks): all three methods covered with application and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): two methods covered, limited judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic points, no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following describes a closed loop system?
options: A system with no process block
A system with a single input and output
A system where the output is fed back to regulate the input
A system that operates on a fixed timer

knowledge_checks.q: Which representation shows the physical position and copper track routing of components on a board?
In a system block diagram, signal _____ show the direction of information flow between blocks.
A thermostat that switches a boiler on and off based on room temperature is an example of a _____ loop system.
Match each representation method to its primary purpose.
right: Shows component symbols and electrical connections
Shows physical component placement and copper tracks
Shows system function and signal flow with labelled blocks

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three stages in the systems approach used in block diagrams?
flashcard_questions.a: The three stages are input, process, and output, with signal arrows showing direction of information flow.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between an open loop and a closed loop system?
flashcard_questions.a: A closed loop system has a feedback path from output back to input; an open loop system has none.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a circuit schematic show that a block diagram does not?
flashcard_questions.a: A circuit schematic shows the actual component types and their electrical connections using standard symbols.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a PCB layout show that a schematic does not?
flashcard_questions.a: A PCB layout shows the physical position of components and the routing of copper tracks on the board.

flashcard_questions.q: Give an example of an open loop system and explain why it is open loop.
flashcard_questions.a: A microwave set to run for two minutes is open loop because the food temperature does not feed back to stop it.

flashcard_questions.q: Give an example of a closed loop system and identify the feedback signal.
flashcard_questions.a: A thermostat is closed loop; room temperature feeds back to the controller to switch the boiler on or off.

flashcard_questions.q: What do signal arrows on a block diagram represent?
flashcard_questions.a: Signal arrows show the direction in which information or signals travel between blocks in the system.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the maximum number of system blocks the OCR specification requires you to interpret?
flashcard_questions.a: The OCR specification requires interpretation of block diagrams with a maximum of four system blocks.

flashcard_questions.q: What do reference designators such as R1 and C1 identify on a PCB layout?
flashcard_questions.a: Reference designators identify individual components: R1 is the first resistor and C1 is the first capacitor.

flashcard_questions.q: At what stage of the design process is a block diagram most useful?
flashcard_questions.a: A block diagram is most useful at the early concept stage before specific components have been chosen.

flashcard_questions.q: Where does the feedback arrow point in a closed loop block diagram?
flashcard_questions.a: The feedback arrow points from the output block back towards the input or process block.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a schematic needed if a block diagram already shows the system?
flashcard_questions.a: A schematic specifies exact component types and connections, which are essential for building and testing the circuit.
